A professional restoration house will charge you $40 per hour of VHS at the cheap end and up to $600 per 15 minutes of 4K restoration at the high end — roughly $1,200 to $2,400 for a single hour of finished footage. Or you buy AI video enhancers 2026 and do it on your own GPU for a one-time license fee. This is a buyer's guide for people who have old footage and don't want to pay Hollywood rates to save it.

I tested four products people actually reach for — Topaz Video AI, AVCLabs Video Enhancer AI, HitPaw Video Enhancer, and CapCut — and I'm going to tell you which one to buy, which one to skip, and which one you already own. Spoiler: the answer depends less on the software and more on your GPU, your footage, and whether you plan to do this once or forever.

## What AI video enhancers 2026 actually fix

Before you spend anything, understand the job. AI video enhancers 2026 do four distinct things, and each one is a separate model with separate strengths:

**Upscaling.** This is the headline feature. The tool takes 480p or 720p source and reconstructs a 1080p or 4K frame by predicting detail that isn't really there. Topaz calls its models Proteus, Iris, Gaia and Theia. AVCLabs uses a transformer-based pipeline. HitPaw has an animation model that handles flat colors and hard lines better than anything else in this list. Every serious AI video upscaler claims 4K output; the difference is how much edge haloing and flicker you get in motion. And if your job is to upscale old video footage shot on tape or an early smartphone, the desktop tools are the only ones worth your time — the online freebies stretch pixels and call it AI.

**Denoising and deblurring.** Old tape and phone footage carry grain, compression artifacts and motion blur. The denoise pass cleans the grain *before* upscaling — run it after and you're just sharpening noise. This is the single biggest quality lever, and it's why the "AI" in these tools matters. Bicubic scaling can't do this.

**Deinterlacing.** If your footage came from a camcorder or TV capture, every frame is actually two half-frames scanned at different times. Interlaced video looks like a comb on modern screens. All three desktop tools deinterlace; CapCut mostly doesn't.

**Frame interpolation.** This creates new frames between existing ones — 24fps footage becomes 60fps, which is what you want for smooth slow motion from standard-rate source. Topaz's Chronos and Apollo models are the reference here; HitPaw and AVCLabs have interpolation models too, but their output is softer on fast motion.

Now the hard truth nobody puts in a feature list: **an enhancer cannot invent detail that the source never contained.** A 320p YouTube rip that's been re-encoded three times is mostly gone. Upscaling it gives you a bigger, blurrier file. The tools work best on footage with real structure — VHS, MiniDV, 1080p phone footage, AI-generated clips — not on compressed garbage. If you're trying to fix a WhatsApp-forwarded video, stop now. That's not what video restoration software does.

One more thing: these are enhancers, not editors and not generators. If you need to cut, caption, or trim, you want an editor — see our [AI video editing tools](/articles/best-ai-video-editing-tools-2026-descript-vs-capcut-vs-veed-vs-kapwing/) roundup. If you need to *create* footage from text, that's a different category entirely — [AI video generation tools](/articles/best-ai-video-generation-tools-2026-runway-vs-pika-vs-kling-vs-luma/) — and enhancers are the right follow-up step for the 720p output those generators produce.

## Topaz Video AI — the quality benchmark, if your GPU can take it

Topaz Video AI is the professional standard for upscaling and restoration, and every other product in this category positions itself against it. It runs entirely on your machine — nothing leaves your computer, which matters if the footage is a client's. It upscales to 8K, deinterlaces, denoises, deblurs, stabilizes, and interpolates frames, and its temporal models keep frames consistent so you don't get the flicker that image-based upscalers produce when applied to video.

**Topaz Video AI pricing** is the most important number here: $299 one-time, which includes a year of model updates. After that, the software keeps working forever; you only pay again ($99/year) if you want newer models. Compare that to the $1,200 to $2,400 an hour a restoration service charges, and the license pays for itself on the first real job. That's not marketing math, that's the price list of actual restoration vendors I checked.

The catch is hardware. Topaz recommends an NVIDIA GPU with at least 4GB of VRAM; an RTX 3060 or better is the practical floor. Apple Silicon Macs work and perform well, but a MacBook Air will crawl on 4K output. If you want an AI video enhancer for Mac with serious power, budget for an M-series Pro or Max chip or an external GPU. Integrated graphics will technically run, but a 10-minute clip can take hours — preview before committing, and don't skip the grain-removal pass.

Who should buy it: anyone with recurring restoration work — wedding editors delivering 4K from 1080p source, archivists, people monetizing old footage libraries. Who shouldn't: someone with one family tape and a laptop without a discrete GPU. You'd be buying a race car for a grocery run. And if your archive is mostly stills instead of motion, [Topaz Photo AI](/tools/topaz-photo-ai/) is the photo-side counterpart — same company, same approach, one frame at a time.

## AVCLabs Video Enhancer AI — the easier rival with the better faces

AVCLabs is the main alternative, and the direct **Topaz Video AI vs AVCLabs** comparison comes down to workflow versus ceiling. AVCLabs runs on Windows, macOS, and has a cloud version — no GPU required if you use the cloud tier. Its interface is simpler than Topaz's: import, pick a model, export. Its standout is face refinement: in side-by-side tests of a blurry 360p home video, AVCLabs reconstructed facial features that other tools turned into smooth blobs.

Pricing: $39.95/month, $119.95/year (frequently discounted to about $96), or a perpetual license that lists at $299.90 but routinely drops to $149.90 on sale. There's a free version with a watermarked 30-second export limit, so you can test your actual footage before paying. The free trial alone makes it worth installing if you're comparing tools.

The tradeoffs: quality on extreme restoration is a notch below Topaz in most shootouts, especially on film grain and motion. Fast-moving scenes can show edge smoothing artifacts. And the subscription price is steep if you only have one project — the perpetual license on sale is the only plan that makes sense for a one-off.

## HitPaw Video Enhancer — for beginners and anime

HitPaw Video Enhancer (now branded VikPea) is the one-click option. Upload, pick a model, preview three seconds, export. It has specialized models — General Denoise, Face, Animation, Colorize, Color Enhancement, Frame Interpolation, Stabilize, Low-light — and its animation model is genuinely good, often beating Topaz on flat-color content like cartoons and game captures. For family archivists colorizing black-and-white home movies, the Colorize model does a respectable job with zero learning curve.

Pricing is the weak point: $42.99/month, $99.99/year, or $349.99 lifetime — the most expensive perpetual license in this comparison, and there's no free export at all, just a 3-second preview. One license covers one PC. HitPaw also can't apply multiple models in one pass; upscaling and colorizing means running the video twice.

Who should buy it: non-technical users, anime fans, and people doing one-off family restorations who won't touch advanced settings. Who shouldn't: anyone processing more than a few clips, because the price and the double-pass workflow add up fast.

## CapCut — the free option you already have

CapCut is not a restoration tool. It's a social video editor with light enhancement features — sharpen, denoise, and 4K upscaling presets inside its Magic Studio. But if your goal is "make this clip look less terrible for a Reel," it's genuinely the best value: the free tier exports up to 1080p with watermarks on some premium effects, and [CapCut](/tools/capcut-ai/) Pro runs about $10 to $20 per month depending on region and billing cycle (pricing was restructured in May 2025, so check capcut.com rather than trusting any third-party list).

The limits are real: no serious deinterlacing, no frame interpolation beyond basic slow-motion, and upscaling quality is a distant third behind the desktop tools. CapCut is the answer to "I need to improve this phone clip for TikTok," not "I need to restore 200 hours of MiniDV." For that heavier job, budget for one of the desktop tools below.

## Head-to-head: the honest comparison table

| Product | Price model | Max output | GPU needed | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Topaz Video AI | $299 one-time + $99/yr optional updates | 8K | Yes (NVIDIA 4GB+ VRAM recommended; Apple Silicon OK) | Pros restoring/upscaling lots of footage, archival work |
| AVCLabs Video Enhancer AI | $39.95/mo, $119.95/yr, or ~$150-300 perpetual | 8K | No (cloud tier) / yes (desktop) | Beginners wanting face refinement, one-off projects on perpetual sale |
| HitPaw Video Enhancer | $42.99/mo, $99.99/yr, $349.99 lifetime | 8K | Yes | Anime, colorization, non-technical users |
| CapCut | Free (1080p, some watermarks) / Pro ~$10-20/mo | 4K upscale presets | No | Quick social clips, testing before you commit |

The ROI read is simple: one-time desktop licenses (Topaz, AVCLabs perpetual on sale) win if you process more than a handful of clips. Subscriptions (AVCLabs monthly, HitPaw) only make sense for short bursts of work. CapCut free tier is the zero-cost way to find out if you even need a real enhancer.

## Cost math: what "restore old home videos with AI" really costs

Let me put real numbers on this, because the pricing pages hide the actual economics. A typical 10-minute 1080p home video with moderate noise, sent to a professional service, runs $150 to $400 depending on the vendor — that's the range I found across current restoration price lists, from $5.50/minute basic cleanup to $12.50/minute 4K restoration. VHS-grade transfer and cleanup runs $40 per hour of tape at the budget end. Film archives charge far more.

Now run that same 10-minute clip through Topaz on an RTX 3060: roughly 30 to 60 minutes of render time, some electricity, and if you already own the license, essentially $0 per job. The license amortizes to near-zero after your first full restoration. If you're restoring a wedding archive or a deceased parent's tape collection — 10, 20, 50 hours of footage — the professional route is $5,000 to $50,000. The software route is $299 once, plus your GPU and your time. That's the entire argument for buying one of these tools, and it's why this category exists at all.

The hidden cost is your GPU. If you don't own one with decent VRAM, the cheapest real path is AVCLabs' cloud tier (no hardware needed) or buying a used RTX 3060 before you buy the software. A $200 used GPU plus a $299 license still beats $5,000 of professional restoration on a 50-tape project.

## How to enhance low quality video without losing your weekend

If you want to actually upscale video to 4K or fix a blurry clip, the workflow is the same across all three desktop tools:

1. **Digitize first.** If your source is tape, capture it at the highest quality your deck supports *before* any enhancement. Enhancement can't recover what the capture step threw away.
2. **Denoise before you upscale.** Grain removal first, then upscaling. The reverse order just sharpens the noise. This is the #1 amateur mistake.
3. **Preview on a 10-second slice.** Render a short section with your chosen model before committing to a full export. A wrong setting on a 10-minute clip wastes 30 to 90 minutes of GPU time.
4. **Match the model to the content.** Animation footage wants an animation model. Interlaced camcorder tape wants a deinterlace model first. Faces in low resolution want a face model. The generic "upscale" preset is the worst option for everything.
5. **Export at the resolution you'll actually use.** 1080p → 4K is where the visible gain lives. 4K → 8K is mostly wasted for YouTube and phones.

That's the whole process. Thirty minutes to learn, then it's batch work — load a folder, apply the same settings, walk away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Topaz Video AI worth it in 2026?

If you have recurring restoration work, yes — $299 one-time beats $1,200 to $2,400 per hour of professional restoration on the first big job, and the software keeps working after the included update year ends. If you have one tape and no GPU, no. Run the free trials first: Topaz offers a watermarked trial on most releases, and AVCLabs' free version lets you export 30-second watermarked clips to judge the actual result on your footage.

### Can AI restore old home videos with AI? I mean, really restore them?

Within limits. AI can remove grain, deinterlace, stabilize shake, sharpen faces, and upscale old home videos with AI to 4K — that's real and impressive on tape or MiniDV source. It cannot bring back detail that was never recorded, and heavily compressed re-encoded files stay mushy no matter what you pay. The degradation ceiling is the source tape's generation, not the software's skill.

### What is the best free AI video enhancer?

CapCut's free tier is the most capable zero-cost option for short social clips, with light sharpen, denoise and upscale presets and 1080p export (some watermarks on premium effects). AVCLabs' free version adds a 30-second watermarked export — enough to test your footage before buying. There is no truly free desktop restoration tool that rivals Topaz; treat "free" as a trial, not a product.

### Do I need a powerful GPU for video upscaling?

For the desktop tools, yes — that's the real system requirement. Topaz recommends an NVIDIA card with 4GB+ VRAM, and renders can run many times the clip length on weak hardware. Apple Silicon Macs work, and M-series Pro/Max chips handle it well. If you have no GPU, AVCLabs' cloud tier is the only desktop-brand option that runs without local hardware.

### Should I use an enhancer or an editor?

Both, in that order. Enhance first (denoise, deinterlace, upscale), then edit (cut, caption, export). Running an editor's built-in upscale on already-degraded footage gives you a bigger version of the same problem. If you're starting from AI-generated clips, upscale them after generation, before you cut — that workflow is why [AI video generation tools](/articles/best-ai-video-generation-tools-2026-runway-vs-pika-vs-kling-vs-luma/) and enhancers pair so well.

## Bottom line

Buy Topaz Video AI if you have serious footage and a real GPU — it's the quality ceiling, and the one-time license is the cheapest per-job cost in this category. Choose AVCLabs if you want an easier workflow, cloud processing, or the best face restoration, and grab the perpetual license on sale. Pick HitPaw only if you're a beginner working mostly with anime or single family clips — the price is the worst here. Start with CapCut free if you're not sure you need any of this.

The broader point: AI video enhancers 2026 have turned a $5,000-per-project professional service into a $299 tool you run on your own machine. Reshooting isn't the only option anymore, and for archival, wedding, or family footage, it was never the right one. Test your worst clip on a watermarked trial before you pay for anything — the tools will tell you quickly whether your footage is worth saving. Most of it is. Some of it isn't. Either way, you'll know for the price of a weekend.

title: Best AI Chatbot Builders 2026: Chatbase vs Voiceflow vs Botpress vs Coze — The Real Cost of Hiring a Developer to Build a Bot
description: Around $11-13 billion will move through the chatbot market this year, and roughly 30% of customer service cases are already resolved by software. A custom-built bot runs $20,000-80,000 plus 15-20% annual maintenance; Chatbase, Voiceflow, Botpress, and Coze ship the same outcome for $0-150 a month. This comparison covers real pricing, billing-model traps, ROI math, and who should buy what.
keywords: best chatbot builder for small business
content:
Around $11-13 billion will move through the chatbot market this year, and roughly 30% of customer service cases are already resolved by software, not humans, according to Salesforce. That number is heading toward 50% by 2027. The businesses capturing that shift are not the ones paying $20,000-80,000 for custom-built bots. They are the ones picking a platform and shipping in a week. This guide is a straight comparison of the four platforms that dominate the **AI chatbot builders 2026** conversation — Chatbase, Voiceflow, Botpress, and Coze — with real pricing, real limits, and the math that decides which one pays for itself. If you are evaluating any no-code chatbot builder this year, these four are the benchmark everything else gets measured against.

## The AI chatbot builders 2026 landscape: four ways to spend your money

Every chatbot platform sells the same promise — a bot that answers questions from your own content — but the four leaders here charge for it in completely different ways, and that difference matters more than any feature list. Chatbase bills by message credits, Voiceflow bills by AI credits plus editor seats, Botpress switched to conversation-based pricing in May 2026, and Coze runs on a daily credit allowance. If you pick the wrong billing model for your traffic, the bill can swing from $150 to $1,500 a month without a single user complaining. Most chatbot platform pricing comparison write-ups are useless for the same reason: they compare sticker prices, not the unit economics of your actual conversation volume.

Let me be blunt about where each one fits before we get to the numbers. Chatbase is the fastest path from "I have a knowledge base" to "the bot is live" — upload files, embed a widget, done. Voiceflow is the design tool of the category; if you want a drag-and-drop canvas that product teams can argue over like a Figma file, that is the pick. Botpress is the developer's option, with an open-source core and self-hosting, and it repriced itself hard in 2026. Coze is the budget play with a real free tier, owned by ByteDance, which brings both cheap credits and a compliance conversation you need to have before you sign up.

## Chatbase: the fastest bot you will ever ship

Chatbase is built around retrieval-augmented generation on your own data. You point it at PDFs, website URLs, Notion exports, or a knowledge base, and it produces a working widget in under ten minutes. No flow builder, no decision trees — the model answers from your content and hands off to a human when it cannot. That simplicity is the whole product, and it is why small teams keep choosing it.

The pricing is credit-based and it escalates fast. The free plan gives you 50 message credits a month — enough to test, nothing more. Hobby runs $40/month (or $32 billed annually) for 500 credits and two members. Standard is $150/month ($120 annually) for 4,000 credits, API access, and voice telephony. Pro is $500/month ($400 annually) for 15,000 credits and advanced analytics. Overages cost $40 per 1,000 credits, removing the "Powered by Chatbase" branding is $99/month, and a second agent is $25/month. The trap here is volume: a support bot that answers 200 questions a day burns roughly 4,000-6,000 credits a month, which silently pushes you from Standard toward Pro faster than the feature list suggests.

## Voiceflow: the design tool that scales with teams

Voiceflow approaches the same problem from the opposite direction. Instead of "upload content and go," it gives you a visual conversation canvas where flows, branches, and LLM calls are built block by block. That makes it the strongest choice when designers and product managers need to collaborate on the bot, and it is the reason Turo, StubHub, and Rocket Mortgage show up in its case studies. It also makes it slower to launch: you are designing, not just uploading.

Voiceflow's pricing tiers are Pro at $60/month (10,000 credits, up to 20 agents, GPT-4 and Claude access) and Team at $150/month (30,000 credits, unlimited agents, 15 concurrent voice calls). Every extra editor seat costs $50/month, and annual billing saves 10%. Credits do not roll over, and heavy LLM workflows — the kind that hit the knowledge base on every turn — can drain 10,000 credits in days, not weeks. For a solo operator this is a lot of platform for the money, but the moment you add collaborators the per-seat math gets aggressive. And when you hear the Voiceflow vs Botpress debate, understand it as a team question: Voiceflow wins when a design team owns the bot, Botpress wins when developers do.

## Botpress: the developer platform that repriced itself

Botpress is the open-source heavyweight, with a codebase carrying over 14,700 GitHub stars and roughly 600,000 developers in its orbit, including teams at Kia and Electronic Arts. The headline feature is choice: you can run it in the cloud or self-host the MIT-licensed version with zero conversation limits. For companies with data-residency requirements, that option alone justifies the platform.

The May 2026 repricing moved Botpress from message-based to conversation-based billing and folded AI usage into every paid tier. Free gives you 100 conversations a month. Plus is $150/month for 250 conversations, three seats, and unlimited bots, with overage packs at $65 per 100 conversations. Team is $750/month for 1,500 conversations and unlimited seats. The unit economics are brutal if you have real traffic — 250 conversations is a slow Tuesday for an active support bot — but the self-hosted path remains completely free, which keeps Botpress relevant for technical teams who would rather pay in engineering hours than in platform fees.

## Coze: the free tier that is actually free

Coze is ByteDance's answer, and it changes the pricing conversation entirely. The Coze free plan gives you 10 credits a day, five collaborators, and three bots — genuinely usable for testing and light production. Paid tiers start at $9/month for 100 credits a day, $19/month for 400, and $39/month for 1,000. You get GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini access plus a 60+ plugin ecosystem, all inside a visual workflow builder with multi-channel publishing to Discord, Telegram, Slack, and the web.

The catch is the owner. ByteDance runs both coze.com and the separate coze.cn, and the two products have different feature sets and data handling. If your business has any policy against China-based data processing — government work, defense, some regulated industries — Coze is ruled out before you look at features. For everyone else, it is the cheapest production-capable builder in this comparison, and the daily credit system is easier to budget than message credits because the clock resets every day rather than every month.

## The pricing table nobody shows you

| Platform | Entry cost | What you actually pay for | Real-world bill at 5,000 convs/mo | Best fit |
|----------|-----------|---------------------------|-----------------------------------|----------|
| Chatbase | Free / $32-40 | Message credits + overages ($40/1K) | ~$150-400 (Standard/Pro) | Non-technical teams shipping a support bot in days |
| Voiceflow | Free / $60 | AI credits + $50/extra editor seat | ~$60-150 + seat costs | Product teams designing conversational flows |
| Botpress | Free / $150 | Conversations ($65-50 per 100 overage) | ~$750+ or $0 self-hosted | Developers wanting control or self-hosting |
| Coze | Free / $9 | Daily credits (10-1,000/day) | ~$9-39 | Budget builders without data-residency constraints |

## What the ROI math actually says

Here is the number that should anchor every buying decision in this category: the custom chatbot development cost. A custom-built AI chatbot with NLP and CRM integrations runs $20,000-80,000 from an agency, plus 15-20% of that cost per year in maintenance, per 2026 marketplace data from Clutch, Upwork, and Fiverr. The cheapest path to a production bot in this list — Coze at $19/month — costs $228 a year. Even Chatbase's Standard plan at $120/month annually is $1,440 a year, and it includes voice, helpdesk, and API access that a custom build would bill as separate line items.

Run that against the payoff. Most chatbot ROI figures you see quoted come from vendor surveys, so treat them as midpoints rather than promises — but the direction is consistent across sources. Businesses deploying chatbots report an average return of about $3.50 for every dollar invested, with top performers reaching 8x, and the cost of a support interaction drops by roughly 30% once AI deflection kicks in. A $1,440-a-year Chatbase plan that deflects even 400 tickets a year — at a conservative $5 per ticket in agent time — pays for itself with room to spare. The **AI chatbot builders 2026** market is not a place to be cheap for the sake of it; it is a place where the wrong platform choice burns a month of setup time and the right one pays back inside a quarter.

One more number worth quoting, because it is the one people forget: maintenance. A custom bot costs 15-20% of its build price every year just to keep running — model updates, integration fixes, knowledge refreshes. On a $50,000 build that is $7,500-10,000 a year of ongoing spend that no one budgets for, and the platform subscriptions in this guide include all of it. When your CFO asks why you are paying $150 a month for something a developer "could have built," the honest answer is that the developer's version costs $50,000 up front, takes four months, and still needs $10,000 a year in upkeep. That is the trade this entire category is built on, and it is not close.

## Who should buy what

If you need the best chatbot builder for small business specifically, the answer depends on who will run the bot — and the next four picks are ordered for that question.

- **Pick Chatbase** if you are non-technical, you have support docs or a knowledge base sitting around, and you want a live bot before the week ends. The credit model punishes high volume, so watch your usage for the first month.
- **Pick Voiceflow** if your bot is a product — multi-channel flows, voice, complex branching — and a designer or PM needs to own it. Budget for editor seats up front.
- **Pick Botpress** if you have engineering resources and either want to self-host for compliance reasons or expect conversation volume that makes the $150 entry tier uneconomic. The free self-hosted path is the best deal in the category if you can run it.
- **Pick Coze** if budget dominates and your data-handling policy allows it. The $9-19 tiers are a rounding error next to the alternatives, and the free tier is good enough to validate the whole project before spending anything.

And if your actual problem is phone calls instead of chat, the same builders feed into a different conversation — our comparison of [AI voice agents](/articles/best-ai-voice-agents-2026-vapi-vs-retell-vs-bland-vs-twilio/) covers Vapi, Retell, and Bland, while our [AI customer service tools](/articles/best-ai-customer-service-tools-2026-intercom-fin-vs-zendesk-ai-vs-tidio-vs-ada/) guide covers the Intercom Fin and Zendesk route for teams that want a full helpdesk attached. For the broader question of what else a non-technical operator can ship without code, our [no-code AI app builders](/articles/best-no-code-ai-app-builders-non-programmers-2026/) piece is the right read.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Chatbase or Voiceflow better for a small business?

For a small business with no developer on staff, Chatbase wins almost every time: upload your docs, embed the widget, and the bot is live in under ten minutes, whereas Voiceflow requires designing a conversation flow first. The [Chatbase vs Voiceflow](/tools/voiceflow/) decision only flips in favor of Voiceflow when you have a design or product team that needs to iterate on the bot itself, and you are willing to spend the first week building flows instead of shipping.

### Can I use Botpress for free?

Yes, on two levels. The cloud free plan gives you 100 conversations a month — fine for testing. The bigger answer is the self-hosted MIT-licensed version, which runs with no conversation limits at all; you pay in engineering hours for deployment, updates, and hosting instead of in platform fees. That is the Botpress self-hosted route most cost-sensitive developers take, and it is why Botpress stays relevant next to cheaper cloud options like [Coze](/tools/coze/).

### How much does it cost to build a chatbot with custom development?

Agencies charge $20,000-80,000 for an AI chatbot with integrations, freelance developers bill $40-200 an hour, and maintenance adds 15-20% of the build cost per year. For a typical small-business bot handling support and lead capture, the three-year total is roughly $65,000-70,000. Every platform in this guide delivers the same outcome for under $2,000 a year, which is why custom development only makes sense for genuinely specialized use cases.

### What is the cheapest AI chatbot builder in 2026?

Coze has the cheapest real plan at $9/month for 100 daily credits, and its free tier (10 credits a day, three bots) is genuinely usable for website deployment on a low-traffic site. Chatbase's Hobby tier at $32-40/month is the cheapest for a support bot trained on your own documents, but message credits run out quickly under real traffic — budget for the Standard tier if you expect more than a few hundred conversations a month.

### How many conversations does a small business chatbot handle per month?

A typical AI chatbot for website deployment sees 500-5,000 conversations a month depending on traffic and how aggressively the widget is pushed. At 1,000 conversations, Chatbase needs Standard ($150), Voiceflow needs 10,000 credits which Pro covers, Botpress burns through its 250-conversation Plus tier and requires overage packs, and Coze's 400-credit daily allowance handles it comfortably at $19/month. This is the math that decides which platform is actually cheap for you.

## Bottom Line

The **AI chatbot builders 2026** category has settled into four distinct answers: Chatbase for speed, Voiceflow for design, Botpress for control, and Coze for cost. None of them is objectively the best, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. What is objective is the arithmetic: a custom build costs $20,000-80,000 and takes months, while every option here costs less than $2,000 a year and ships in days. Start with the free tier of whichever platform matches your team, measure your real conversation volume for a month, and upgrade based on that number — not on a feature checklist. The businesses winning the chatbot game in 2026 are not the ones with the most sophisticated bots. They are the ones that shipped first and let the data tell them where to go next. For more context on where this category sits in the wider tool market, our [best AI tools for small business](/articles/ai-tools-for-small-business-2026/) roundup is a good next stop.

title: Best AI Photo Enhancers in 2026: Topaz Photo AI vs Remini vs Gigapixel vs Upscayl — The Real Cost of Restoring Old Photos
description: Professional photo restoration labs charge $50-150 per image for standard work and $200-500+ for heavy damage. AI photo enhancers 2026 cut that to a one-time software license or a free open-source app. This comparison covers Topaz Photo AI, Remini, Gigapixel AI, and Upscayl — real pricing, billing traps, hardware requirements, and the ROI math for restoring a 200-photo family album.
content:
Professional photo restoration labs charge $50-150 per image for standard work, and $200-500+ when a photo has real damage — torn corners, water stains, a face faded past recognition. AI photo enhancers 2026 have collapsed that cost to a one-time software purchase that pays for itself on the first dozen photos. This guide compares the four options people actually run — Topaz Photo AI, Remini, Topaz Gigapixel AI, and the open-source freebie Upscayl — with current pricing, honest limits, and the math for restoring a full family album instead of a single frame.

The numbers behind the hype are worth pinning down first. Studios surveyed across 12 countries charge $8-15 per photo for light restoration, $20-40 for moderate damage, and $50-90 for heavy damage — and those are the volume rates (restoregram.com, 2026). One-off professional labs run $50-150 for standard work, $150-300 for complex jobs, and conservation-grade work starts around $200 (artimagehub.com, 2026). Demand is not slowing down: more than 30 million Americans are now over 80, and estate sales are pushing 500-2,000 photos per family through restoration shops. AI-assisted studios move 150-300 images a day with two staff; fully manual shops manage 20-30 (restoregram.com, 2026). The cost gap between those two columns is exactly what the software below is selling into. If you want to restore old photos with AI without a single per-photo bill, the one-time tools in this roundup are where that math starts.

## AI photo enhancers 2026: the four realistic options

### Topaz Photo AI — the $199 one-time license

Topaz Photo AI is the closest thing to a restoration lab in a box. The one-time license costs $199 and includes one year of model updates; after that you keep the software forever, and a $99-per-year plan buys new models when they ship. For that money you get upscaling to 6x, noise removal, sharpening, and face recovery in a single app, plus an Autopilot mode that looks at each photo and applies the right pass automatically. In a 100-photo benchmark against Adobe Super Resolution, Gigapixel AI, ON1 Resize, Let's Enhance, and Upscayl, it ranked first for detail quality, face recovery, and cleanest noise removal (hashmeta.ai, 2026). There is a 30-day money-back window, and the trial gives unlimited watermarked previews, so you can test it on your own scans before paying.

Two conditions decide whether Topaz works for you. First, it is desktop-only — Windows or macOS, no web app, no phone version — and it wants a GPU with at least 4GB of VRAM, ideally 8GB or more. On Apple Silicon it runs well; on Intel Macs without a discrete GPU it falls back to CPU and takes 1-3 minutes per image, which is fine for a few dozen photos and painful for a few hundred. Second, it is a specialist, not an editor. There is no catalog, no color grading, no background removal. You fix the technical problems here, then finish the job in your normal editor. If you want the full picture on where it fits, the [Topaz Photo AI tool page](/tools/topaz-photo-ai/) has a longer review.

The break-even math is short. Restore a box of 200 family photos yourself and the professional alternative is $8-90 per photo depending on damage — call it $1,600-18,000 for the box. Topaz at $199 covers all 200, plus the next 200, plus a side gig if you want one. The people who regret the purchase are usually the ones who bought it for a single photo of a grandparent and never touched it again.

### Remini — the face fixer with a billing trap

Remini is the mass-market option, and it is genuinely good at the one thing most people care about: faces. It is a mobile-first app from Bending Spoons that has run Google's Gemini Flash Image model since November 2025 — weekly installs jumped 175% to about 1.16 million after that switch. Total downloads passed 100 million, it crossed a billion enhanced photos back in 2023, and as of June 2026 it sits at roughly 15.6 million monthly active users, the 31st most-used AI app in the world (AICPB, 2026). For a casual user who wants an old portrait sharp enough to print, one tap in Remini beats anything desktop-only.

The free tier gives you a few enhancements a day with ads and a watermark. Paid plans run about $5-10 a week, roughly $20 a month, or $72-80 a year depending on region and app store — the Remini subscription cost swings a lot between iOS and Android, so check the in-app price before committing. Here is the trap: the weekly plan auto-renews, and $9.99 a week is $519 a year if you forget to cancel, which is more than six times the annual plan. Remini's Trustpilot score sits around 1.3-1.5 stars, and the complaint pattern is almost entirely billing rather than output quality — one user reported ten weekly charges after ending a free trial. Set a calendar reminder the same day you subscribe.

Two honest limits. Remini is weak on non-portrait content: landscapes, product shots, and documents come out over-processed, because the whole model is tuned for faces. And its AI face enhancement invents detail — that restored portrait looks convincing, but it is not a faithful record of what the negative actually captured. For grandma's birthday print that is fine. For anything where accuracy matters, it is the wrong tool.

### Topaz Gigapixel AI — upscaling only, half the price

Gigapixel AI is the same upscaling engine that powers Photo AI, sold on its own at $99.99 one-time with up to 6x enlargement, batch processing, and a much simpler interface. If your images are already clean — properly exposed, already sharp — and you just need them bigger, Gigapixel delivers the same enlargement quality for $100 less than Photo AI. The classic reason to upscale old photos for printing is a wall-size enlargement — a wedding portrait scanned at 2MP does not survive a 24-inch print without AI-generated texture. The trade-off is real: no noise removal and no sharpening. A noisy source stays noisy, just larger; a soft image stays soft. If your photos need more than size, the extra $100 for Photo AI buys denoise and sharpen modules that cost more than that when bought separately as DeNoise AI and Sharpen AI.

### Upscayl — the free option that is actually good

Upscayl is open-source, free forever, and runs entirely on your own machine using Real-ESRGAN models. For 4x upscaling of reasonably clean images, the output is close enough to the paid tools that most people cannot tell the difference without zooming in. No subscriptions, no credits, no watermark, and nothing leaves your computer — which also makes it the privacy answer if you are restoring photos you do not want sitting on someone's server. The trade-offs: it needs a capable GPU or it crawls, it only does upscaling (no face recovery, no noise removal), and the interface is one button rather than a workflow. Upscayl ships native builds for Windows, macOS, and Linux, which makes it a reasonable AI photo enhancer for Mac users who are not ready to pay for Topaz. If your entire job is making old scans bigger so they print well, this is the honest answer at $0.

## The math: what restoring a real photo collection costs

For a single family, the break-even math for AI photo enhancers 2026 is brutal in your favor. The Topaz Photo AI vs Remini decision comes down to hardware and volume: a GPU and a hundred photos points to Topaz, while a phone and five priority photos points to Remini. Take 200 photos with typical age-related damage — fading, dust, light scratches. Through a professional lab at volume rates that is $1,600-18,000 depending on how many photos fall into the moderate and heavy tiers. Through an AI restoration service that charges $5-20 per photo (artimagehub.com, 2026), it is $1,000-4,000 and you wait days, not weeks. Through Topaz Photo AI on a GPU you own, it is $199 and a weekend of batch processing. Through Upscayl, $0 and as long as your patience holds.

| Tool | Price model | Best at | Biggest weakness | Cost for 200 photos |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Topaz Photo AI | $199 one-time (+$99/yr optional updates) | All-in-one upscale, denoise, sharpen, face recovery | Desktop only, needs a real GPU | $199 |
| Remini | Free with ads; $5-10/wk, ~$20/mo, $72-80/yr | Face and portrait restoration on your phone | Weekly auto-renew trap; invents facial detail | $72-519 |
| Topaz Gigapixel AI | $99.99 one-time | Pure 6x upscaling of clean images | No denoise, no sharpening | $99.99 |
| Upscayl | Free (open source) | 4x local upscaling, private by design | Needs GPU, no face or noise features | $0 |
| Professional lab | $50-150 per photo (standard work) | Complex damage, museum-grade output | Slow turnaround, expensive at volume | $10,000-30,000 |

The side-gig angle is where the numbers stop being theoretical. Restoration shops are already quoting $8-90 per photo, and AI services charge $5-20. A solo operator with Topaz and a couple of hours a night can restore 15-20 photos an hour, which prices out to $100-300 an hour of work at market rates before marketing time. The demand exists — the estate flood is real — and the marginal cost after the $199 license is zero. That is a legitimate side business for someone who wants one, and it is the reason the one-time license beats every subscription for anyone with a GPU. The AI photo restoration cost story of 2026 is simple: the fixed-cost tools win at any volume above a handful of photos.

## Where AI photo enhancers fail

Be honest about the walls, because the marketing pages do not mention them. First, missing detail cannot be recovered — it gets invented. A hard out-of-focus face will come back with plausible features that were never captured, and no upscaler on the market can create detail the lens did not record. Mild motion blur is fixable; hard misfocus is not, and tools like Remini will silently fill in a face that is not the real one.

Second, the GPU is the hidden tax. Topaz and Upscayl are local-first, which is great for privacy and batch volume, but on a laptop without a discrete GPU you are looking at 1-3 minutes per image. If your hardware is weak and you still have hundreds of photos, a cloud option starts to make sense even with its per-photo cost.

Third, over-sharpening is a real artifact problem. Autopilot-style tools default to aggressive settings; the topaz community guidance is to keep sharpening around 50-70% and inspect every image that will be printed, because edge halos show up fast on white borders.

Fourth, scope. An enhancer is not an editor. If your photos need background removal, product cleanup, or compositing, you are in the wrong category — that is the job of tools like [Photoroom](/tools/photoroom/) and [Remove.bg](/tools/remove.bg/), which we covered in the [photo editing tools comparison](/articles/best-ai-photo-editing-tools-2026-remove-bg-vs-photoroom-vs-adobe-firefly-vs-canva-ai/). And if your actual problem is generating a new headshot rather than fixing an old one, start with our [AI headshot generators guide](/articles/best-ai-headshot-generators-2026-headshotpro-vs-aragon-vs-tryiton-vs-prophotos/) instead.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Remini worth its weekly subscription price?

Only if you have a short burst of work. A single week at $6.99-9.99 handles one family album's worth of priority photos, and you can cancel after the first batch. The moment you are paying weekly for more than a month, the math breaks: $9.99 a week is $519 a year, versus $72-80 for the annual plan. The free tier's few daily enhancements are enough to test whether the output actually helps your photos before you spend anything.

### Can AI photo enhancers fix out-of-focus photos?

Partially, and the distinction matters. Motion blur and light focus misses respond well to sharpening passes — this is the most-used feature in Topaz Photo AI for casual shooters, and for mild cases the dependable way to enhance blurry photos is a sharpen pass held around 50-70% strength. Hard misfocus, where the whole face is soft, cannot be fixed: the tool will invent texture that was not in the frame. On faces specifically, Remini's reconstruction looks impressive and is not a faithful record. If the photo is the only copy of a person's face, keep the original safe and treat the AI output as an artistic version, not the archive.

### Do I need a powerful GPU for AI photo enhancement?

For Topaz and Upscayl, yes — that is the deciding factor between desktop and cloud. Topaz wants 4GB of VRAM minimum and runs much better at 8GB; Apple Silicon machines are fine. On CPU-only hardware, expect 1-3 minutes per image, which is tolerable for a handful and unusable for a collection. Remini does all processing in the cloud, so it is the right pick when your hardware is weak and your job is small.

### Can I sell restored photos as a side business?

Yes, and the market is already priced. Studios quote $8-90 per photo, AI services $5-20, and the demand is backed by the estate flood — estates now deliver 500-2,000 images at a time. A solo operator with a one-time $199 license, a decent GPU, and honest quality control can undercut every lab on price while keeping 90%+ margins. Two rules: never present AI-invented detail as the original, and quote a fixed per-tier price based on damage level before seeing the photos, the same way the studios do.

## Bottom Line

The AI photo enhancers 2026 landscape splits cleanly: pay once, pay weekly, or pay nothing. Topaz Photo AI at $199 is the right call for anyone with a GPU and a real collection — or a side gig in mind — and the one-time license beats every subscription by year two. Gigapixel at $99.99 is the smarter buy if your photos are clean and only need to be larger. Remini is a fine phone app for quick face fixes, provided you cancel the auto-renew the day you subscribe. Upscayl is the free AI photo enhancer that handles the $0 budget and the privacy-sensitive job. And if your photos need background work instead of restoration, those are different tools entirely — see the [photo editing comparison](/articles/best-ai-photo-editing-tools-2026-remove-bg-vs-photoroom-vs-adobe-firefly-vs-canva-ai/) before you buy anything.

title: Best AI Keyword Research Tools in 2026: Ahrefs vs Semrush vs Moz vs Google Keyword Planner — The Real Cost of Data You're Not Using
description: We compared Ahrefs, Semrush, Moz Pro, and Google Keyword Planner on price, database size, AI features, and real-world ROI. Short version: most people pay $129+/month and use about 20% of what they buy. Here's what actually matters.
content:
About 72% of organic search traffic now lands on pages that target long-tail keywords, according to Statista's 2025 Search Marketing Trends report. Meanwhile, 87% of marketers say keyword research is their top SEO priority, and Semrush's own index of 29.3 billion keywords shows that only 0.00076% of them get more than 100,000 searches a month. Read those three numbers together and the picture is clear: the traffic you actually want is spread across thousands of small, specific phrases, not a handful of head terms. That is the entire reason the AI keyword research tools 2026 market exists, and it is also why most people are buying the wrong tool.

I have run SEO for affiliate sites, product pages, and B2B content since 2008. I have paid for Ahrefs, Semrush, and Moz at various points, and I have watched colleagues burn $1,500 a year on subscriptions they barely open. This guide is the comparison I wish someone had written before my first invoice. No affiliate fluff, no "all tools are great" diplomacy. Four tools, real prices, and a straight answer about which one you should actually pay for.

## AI keyword research tools 2026: the market split into two camps

The phrase "AI keyword research tools 2026" covers two very different product families, and the confusion between them is why so many buyers overpay.

**Camp one is data depth.** Ahrefs and Semrush built their businesses on enormous keyword databases, historical search volume, and backlink indexes. Their AI features are add-ons bolted onto a data engine. You pay for the data, and the AI helps you sort it.

**Camp two is AI-first workflow.** The genuinely new thing in the last 18 months is not "AI finds keywords for you." It is tools that cluster thousands of keywords by search intent automatically, score your draft against the top ten results while you write, and — the big one — track whether your content gets cited inside ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity answers. Semrush calls this its AI Visibility Toolkit, Moz ships an AI Visibility Dashboard, and Ahrefs sells it as the Brand Radar add-on at $199 a month.

Here is the uncomfortable truth about that second camp: the AI search visibility tracking is real, but for a small site it is a vanity metric. If you rank nowhere on Google, being "cited by ChatGPT" for zero-traffic prompts earns you nothing. The practical version of long-tail keyword research is still: find 200 phrases with real intent, filter out the ones you cannot win, write pages that answer them, and track what happens. The tool that does that job well — without charging you $199 for a dashboard you will check twice — is the tool you want.

## The four tools, priced like a purchase decision

Let me be direct about pricing, because every review site obfuscates this. Prices below are what I verified from official pricing pages in August 2026. They change, so treat them as a baseline and check the vendor page before you commit.

**Ahrefs** — Free, Starter $29/mo, Lite $129/mo (about $108/mo billed annually), Standard $249/mo ($208 annually), Advanced $449/mo ($374 annually), Enterprise from $1,499. Ahrefs does not offer a free trial and says it never runs discounts. It claims 50,000+ paying customers, including 44% of the Fortune 500. The keyword research strengths are the metrics nobody else has: Parent Topic (whether you can rank for a phrase by targeting a broader topic), Traffic Potential (estimated traffic at rank #1), Return Rate, and Clicks Per Search. The weakness is that the AI layer is an upsell: AI Content Helper runs $99/month for 50 documents on top of your plan.

**Semrush** — Pro $139.95/mo ($117.33 annually), Guru $249.95/mo ($208.33 annually), Business $499.95/mo ($416.66 annually), with a 7-day trial. The Keyword Magic tool sits on a 25+ billion keyword database. Semrush is the only one of the three that auto-clusters keywords by intent out of the box, and its ContentShake AI drafts full articles scored by the SEO Writing Assistant. In a head-to-head test I found, ContentShake drafts averaged 72/100 before editing — a usable start, not publish-ready. New for 2026 is Semrush One, a bundle from $199/mo that adds AI visibility tracking on top of the classic toolkit.

**Moz Pro** — Starter $49/mo, Standard $99/mo ($79 annually, 3 sites, 300 tracked keywords), Medium $179/mo ($143 annually, 10 sites, 1,500 keywords), Large $299/mo ($239 annually, 25 sites, 3,000 keywords). Moz gives you a 30-day free trial, which is the longest of the three. Its Domain Authority metric is still the industry shorthand, and the new AI Keyword Suggestions by Topic feature is genuinely easy for beginners. The cost: the keyword database is smaller, data updates slower, and the backlink index thinner than Ahrefs. Moz Pro pricing is the friendliest of the paid three, and it shows in the feature set.

**Google Keyword Planner** — Free, forever. You need a Google Ads account, but you can create one with "create an account without a campaign" and never spend a cent. The catch that nobody mentions on the marketing page: accounts with no active ad spend only see search volume as ranges (1K–10K), never exact numbers. Google locks precise figures behind roughly $100+/month of active spend, and the threshold is not documented. The "Competition" column measures advertiser competition, not organic difficulty. For zero dollars, it is still the only source of Google's own data, and for seed-term discovery it remains underrated.

| Feature | Ahrefs | Semrush | Moz Pro | Google Keyword Planner |
|--------|--------|---------|---------|------------------------|
| Entry price | $29 (Starter) | $139.95 (Pro) | $49 (Starter) | $0 |
| Mid-tier price | $129 (Lite) | $249.95 (Guru) | $99 (Standard) | Free forever |
| Keyword database | Deep, own crawler | 25B+ indexed | Smaller, slower updates | Google's own data |
| AI features | Content Helper add-on ($99) | Intent clustering + ContentShake | AI Keyword Suggestions + AI Visibility | None |
| Trial / free access | No trial, limited free tools | 7-day trial, 10 queries/day free | 30-day trial | Full tool, ranges only |
| Best fit | Link-focused SEOs | All-in-one marketing teams | Beginners and DA metric fans | $0 budgets and PPC work |

## Where each tool wins — and where it wastes your money

**Buy Ahrefs if you live and die by backlinks and competitor gaps.** The Content Gap tool in Site Explorer is still the fastest way to run competitor keyword analysis: plug in three competitor domains, and it shows you every phrase they rank for that you do not. If you are an agency auditing link profiles, nothing beats it. Waste of money if: your only use is checking a few volumes per week, because Lite at $129/mo buys you 750 tracked keywords you will never fill.

**Buy Semrush if you want one login for SEO plus content plus PPC research.** The Keyword Magic tool, intent clustering, and ContentShake form a workflow that ends in a drafted article. For a small content team that hates tool-hopping, Semrush pricing is justified by consolidation. Waste of money if: you only need keyword research, because you are paying for social scheduling, advertising research, and 55+ tools you will never open.

**Buy Moz Pro if you are new to SEO.** The 30-day trial, the beginner-friendly Keyword Explorer, and the AI Keyword Suggestions by Topic make it the least intimidating paid option, and $99/mo for Standard is the cheapest way to get real keyword difficulty scores and rank tracking. Waste of money if: you need current, complete backlink data — Moz's index is the thinnest of the three.

**Use Google Keyword Planner if your budget is zero.** Pair it with free keyword research tools — Google autocomplete, AnswerThePublic's 3 free searches a day, Ubersuggest's free tier — and you can build a working 200-keyword list without spending anything. The trade-off is real: no keyword difficulty score, no historical data, no competitor gap analysis. You are doing the manual work that $129/month would automate. Most Google Keyword Planner alternatives on the market simply resell the exact numbers Google hides behind ranges, so weigh what you actually need before paying for a reskin.

The pattern across all four: people buy the mid-tier of a suite tool and use one feature. Before you subscribe, write down the three tasks you will actually run weekly. If "check search volume" is the only one, the free stack wins.

## The workflow that actually uses these tools

Here is the sequence I run, which keeps a $0 or $29 budget honest for a solo operator:

1. **Seed with Google Keyword Planner.** Type your product or niche into "Discover new keywords," plus paste in a competitor URL. Google's own index gives you the ground truth on what phrases exist. Ignore the volume ranges; you are mining for phrase patterns, not numbers.
2. **Expand with a real database.** If you have Ahrefs Starter or Semrush's trial, dump your seed list into the keyword explorer. This is where long-tail keyword research happens: filter for 3-to-5-word phrases with volume over a floor you choose, sort by difficulty, and export.
3. **Filter by keyword difficulty score.** Delete everything above the difficulty your domain can win. A fresh site with weak authority has no business targeting KD 60+ terms. This single filter step is where most beginners waste six months.
4. **Verify intent manually.** The tool says "commercial." Your eyes say "blog post about a topic." The tool wins. Check the actual SERP — if the top five results are all product pages, your informational page will not rank there.
5. **Write, publish, track.** Plug the survivors into your rank tracker. Revisit the list quarterly. Keyword decay is real, and tools refresh data monthly.

That last step is where the AI search visibility tracking becomes relevant: once you have pages actually ranking, knowing whether ChatGPT cites you for related prompts is useful signal. Until then it is a distraction.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Google Keyword Planner really free?

Yes, but with a catch. You need a Google Ads account — create one without a campaign and you never enter billing details. The catch is data precision: accounts with no active ad spend see monthly search volume as ranges like "1K–10K" instead of exact numbers. Google unlocks exact figures for accounts spending roughly $100+/month, and it does not publish the threshold. The "Competition" metric is advertiser competition, not organic ranking difficulty. Free, genuinely useful for discovery, and genuinely useless for comparing two similar mid-range keywords.

### Ahrefs vs Semrush: which is better for keyword research?

For pure keyword research, Ahrefs wins on data quality and unique metrics — Parent Topic, Traffic Potential, Return Rate, and Clicks Per Search are genuinely different lenses on the same phrase. Semrush wins on workflow: intent-based keyword clustering and ContentShake AI take you from a keyword list to a drafted article in one platform. The honest answer: Ahrefs is a better data tool, Semrush is a better all-in-one. If you only care about keyword research and nothing else, Ahrefs Starter at $29 is the cheaper entry point — and if you need the full marketing stack, Semrush's breadth justifies its price. Both offer trials or low-cost tiers, so test before committing.

### Are there free AI keyword research tools?

Yes, and the free stack is more capable than most people assume. Google Keyword Planner is the anchor: free, first-party Google data, no credit card. Around it, use Google autocomplete and the related-searches block for phrase patterns, AnswerThePublic (3 free searches a day) for question-based terms, and Ubersuggest's free tier for exact-ish volume and difficulty estimates. Ahrefs also runs a set of free tools — keyword generator, backlink checker, and more — no account required for several of them. The free stack gets you a solid 200-keyword list. What it does not give you: historical data, competitor keyword gap analysis at scale, and automated rank tracking. At some point the manual labor costs more than $29/month.

### How many keywords should I track per month?

Fewer than you think. The paid plans push you toward 500–3,000 tracked keywords, but the solo operators I know get results tracking 50–150. Track only keywords attached to pages that exist and that you are actively optimizing; a tracked keyword with no page targeting it is a number with no action attached. When a page ranks and stabilizes, that is a win to log, not a signal to add more keywords. Scale tracking as your content grows, not before.
